<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - Neko Master is a full-stack, monorepo application for real-time network traffic monitoring, auditing, and visualization.  
   - It consists of two primary services:  
     • Collector (Node.js + Fastify + WebSocket)  
     • Web UI (Next.js + React + TypeScript)  
   - A shared package holds common types/utilities.

2. File Structure Analysis  
   - Top-level directories:  
     • apps/collector – back-end data collector service  
     • apps/web – front-end Next.js application  
     • packages/shared – cross-service utilities and type definitions  
   - Config and deployment artifacts:  
     • Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, setup/start scripts  
     • .env examples and CI workflows  
   - Collector uses a modular MVC-style layout: controllers, services, repositories, schema.  
   - Web app follows Next.js’s app directory structure, with localized pages, shared UI components, hooks, lib, i18n, public assets.

3. Key Architecture Insights from README  
   - Ports: 3000 (Web UI), 3001 (Collector REST API), 3002 (Collector WebSocket)  
   - Frontend proxies `/api` to port 3001 and connects to `/_cm_ws` for real-time updates on 3002.  
   - Data persistence via SQLite (stats.db).  
   - Fallback to HTTP polling (~5s) if WS isn’t available.  
   - Deployment typically via Docker Compose with optional Nginx or Cloudflare Tunnel reverse proxy for unified domain and WS upgrade.

4. Designing the System Diagram  
   a. Main Components (boxes):  
      - Browser (User)  
      - Next.js Frontend (apps/web)  
      - Fastify Collector (apps/collector)  
      - SQLite Database (stats.db)  
      - External Network Gateways (e.g., OpenClash backends)  
      - Shared Library (packages/shared)  
      - Reverse Proxy (Nginx / Cloudflare Tunnel) – optional in production  
   b. Relationships & Data Flow (arrows):  
      1. Browser → HTTP GET `/` → Frontend  
      2. Frontend → HTTP REST → Collector API (port 3001)  
      3. Frontend → WebSocket Upgrade → Collector WS (port 3002)  
      4. Collector ↔ SQLite (read/write stats)  
      5. Collector → Poll/WebSocket request → External Gateways  
      6. Reverse Proxy routes `/` → 3000 and `/_cm_ws` → 3002  
   c. Architectural Patterns & Principles:  
      - Separation of concerns: UI vs. data collection  
      - API Gateway pattern: Next.js acts as a proxy for Collector API  
      - Real-time event streaming with WebSocket + HTTP fallback  
      - Monorepo with shared code to avoid duplication  
      - Modular code organization (controllers/services/repos)  
   d. Key Technologies:  
      - Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, Recharts/D3, next-intl  
      - Backend: Node.js, Fastify, WebSocket, SQLite  
      - Packaging/Deployment: pnpm workspaces, Turbo, Docker Compose, Nginx/Cloudflare

5. Tailoring the Diagram for This Full-Stack App  
   - Draw two service domains side by side:  
     • Frontend (browser, Next.js server)  
     • Backend (Collector service)  
   - Show how the Reverse Proxy sits in front of both for production setups.  
   - Emphasize port mappings and fallback mechanism (WS vs. polling).  
   - Illustrate the data ingestion pipeline: Gateway → Collector → DB → Frontend charts.  
   - Indicate shared package usage by both services.

6. Diagramming Guidelines  
   - Use distinct colors/shapes for each service type:  
     • Blue rectangles for frontend components  
     • Green rectangles for backend components  
     • Orange cylinder for database  
     • Gray clouds for external gateways  
     • Purple box for shared library  
   - Label each box clearly (e.g., “Next.js UI (3000)”, “Fastify API (3001)”, “WebSocket Server (3002)”).  
   - Draw directional arrows with annotated protocols/paths:  
     • “HTTP GET /”  
     • “REST /api → port 3001”  
     • “WS upgrade → /_cm_ws”  
     • “SQLite read/write”  
     • “Polling (5s fallback)”  
   - Group related modules (e.g., collector’s auth, stats, realtime modules) inside the backend box.  
   - Optionally overlay swimlanes or boundary boxes:  
     • Docker container boundaries  
     • PNPM workspace boundary for shared code.

7. Detail and Completeness  
   - Capture all essential components without over-splitting trivial utilities.  
   - Ensure the diagram can be read by both developers and DevOps for deployment.  
   - Verify arrows reflect real network flows and internal dependencies.  
   - Keep labels concise but informative; use a legend for colors/shapes.  
   - Review against the README’s port/env configuration to confirm accuracy.

By following these steps, the system design diagram will clearly and accurately depict Neko Master’s architecture, facilitating onboarding, development planning, and operational deployment.  
</explanation>
